MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 144—Shri Rajnath Singh 'Surya*. 
Journals on defence and strategic studies in Hindi 
†*144. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of 
DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is dearth of magazines and journals 
in Hindi language in the field of defence and strategic studies; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government are implementing any scheme to provide 
information in Hindi with respect to matters related to defence; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, whether Government have any proposal in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): 
(a) and (b) Magazines/Journals/Articles in the field of Defence and strategic 
studies are being published from time to time . The frequency of these 
publications would largely depend on the perceived demand of the target 
Hindi readers. 
(c) to (e) Yes, Sir. Cash award schemes are being implemented to 
encourage Hindi publications of Defenc e related matters. There is a 
Biannual cash award scheme ranging from Rs. ?000 to Rs. 15000 as well 
as an Annual cash award scheme for 'in-house' Hindi publications.

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SHANTA 
KUMAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
The Department of Land Resources (Ministry of Rural Development) is 
implementing three Watershed Development Programmes, namely, the  
Integrated Wasterlands Development Programme (WDP), the Drought Prone Areas 
Programme (DPAP) and the Desert Development Programme (DDP) in Karnataka. 
The Programmes are being implemented through the Watershed Approach, in 
accordance with the Guidelines for Watershed Development which came into 
force in April, 1995; funds are also being provided for the completion of 
Watershed Projects taken up prior to April, 1999 under the Employment 
Assurance Scheme (EAS). 
2. Under the Watershed Development Programmes, no annual 
allocations are made to the States. The budgetary allocations under these 
Programmes are utilized to meet the committed liabilities of ongoing Watershed 
Projects as well as sanction of new projects which are implemented over a 
period of five years, with the total project cost being released in seven 
Instalments. While the first Instalment is released at the time of sanction, each 
subsequent Instalment is released only after ensuring that the unutilised 
balanced of the project is not more than 50% of the previous Instalment 
released.

THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (d) in May, 2001 Defence industry sector, which was hitherto reserved for 
the public sector has been opened upto 100% for Indian Private Sector 
participation with Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), permissible upto 26% 
both subject to licensing.The Indian Private Sector can now manufacture all 
types of defence equipment under licen se. So far the Private Sector was 
involved in the supply of raw material s, semi-finished products, parts and

entrepreneurs:— 
Arms and ammunitions produced by the private manufacturers will be 
primarily sold to the Ministry of Defence.These items may also be sold to 
other Government entities under the control of Ministry of Home Affairs and 
State Government with the prior approval of the Ministry of Defence. No 
such item should be sold within the country to any other person or entity. The 
export of manufactured items would be subject to policy and guidelines as 
applicable to Ordnance Factories and Defence Public Sector Undertakings. 
Non-lethal items would be permitted for sale to persons/ entities other than 
the Central or State Governments with the prior approval of the Ministry of 
Defence.

         (b) The salient features of the one-time settlement scheme and the TPA are: 
1. For the States participating in the scheme, 60% of the interests/

waived off. 
2. The rest of the dues comprising the full principal amount as well

3. The bonds will be issued through RBI at a tax-free interests rate

achieve a moratorium of 5 year on repayment of principal with the 
entire principal being repaid between the 6th and 15th year. These 
bonds should be identical to the bods issued in connection with the 
market borrowings of State Governments with the attendant 
discipline in repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock in 
restrictions that will allow release of only 10 per cent of the bonds 
in the secondary market each year. 
4. For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel to attract a graded reduction in the 
supply of power from central power stations and in coal supplies. 
Payments that remain outstanding after 90 days from the date of billing 
shall be recovered, on behalf of the CPSUs, by the Ministry of 
Finance through adjustment against releases due to the respective 
State Government on account of plan assistance, States' share of 
Central tax and any other grant or

Reforms Commission (SERC), metering of distribution feeders, 
improvement in revenue realisation specified in the Memorandum 
of Understanding (MoU) signed/to be signed with the Ministry of 
Power. 
6. The States to be offered incentives for complying with the scheme. 
If SEBs do not default on their current due and adhere to the 
performance milestones, CPSUs would pay them, bi-annual cash 
incentives equal to 3% of the value of bonds in> the first year, 2.5% in 
the second year and 2% in the third and fourth years (incentive of 
19% for four years). Further, if SEBs open and maintain Letters of 
Credit (LCs), CPSUs would pay them a one time cash incentive 
equal to 2 per cent of value of bonds. In addition, States undertaking 
reforms would also be assisted  through the Accelerated Power 
Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) grants and 
discretionary allocation of Power. 
7. The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this 
scheme enters into force will be denied any share in the 
discretionary allocation of 15 per cent from the power stations of 
CPSUs as well as any assistance under the APDRP. If the overdues 
of such States exceeds Rs. 50 crore in repect of any CPSUs, they

to the States participating in this scheme.

National Body for effective energy policy review 
846. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it was ever considered to form a suitable national body 
comprising of acknowledged experts in the field for an effective "Energy 
Policy Review"; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTIMEHTA): (a) and (b) An Energy Policy Committee 
has been set up in the Planning Commission to recommend an outline of the 
energy policy forthe next 15-20years.The members include Secretaries to the 
Government of India in the Ministries of Power, Coal, Petroleum & Natural Gas, 
Non-Conventional Energy Sources, Environmental & Forests and Department of 
Atomic Energy. Experts from Indira Gandhi Institute of Development 
Research, Tata Energy Rese arch Institute etc. are also associated in the 
Committee. 
Complete Rural electrification in the Country 
†847. SHRI VIJAY SINGH YADAV: W ill the Minister of Power be 
pleased to state: 
(a) by when Government will achieve the target of complete rural 
electrification in the country; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that some of the States are adopting non-
cooperating attitude for the achievement of target; and 
(c) if so, the States which are moving towards in the achievement of target 
of full rural electrification and which are the States lagging behind in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) The Chief Ministers' Conference held on 
3rd March, 2001 had resolved to complete village electrification by the end of 
Tenth Plan i.e. by 2007 and the coverage of all households, by 2012. 
(c) No, Sir. fOriginal notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
(c) At the end of May, 2002, nine States i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Goa, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Kerala, Maharashtra,  Punjab, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu and all 
Union Territories have already achieved 100% village electrification as per 
1991 census. 
Ten States i.e. Himachal Pradesh, J&K, Ka rnataka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Chhattisgarh, Manipur, Mizoram, Nagaland, Rajasthan, Tripura are moving 
towards the achievements of full village electrification. 
Nine States i.e. Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Jharkhand, 
Meghalaya, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal and West Bengal are below 
the national level of 86.7% village electrification. 
The average rural household electrifi cation in the country, as per 1991 
census is 31 %. The States which are below the national average are 
Rajasthan, Tirpura, West Bengal, Orissa, Meghalaya, Assam, U.P., Bihar and 
J&K. All the rural households are target ed for electrification by 2012 and the 
States have reiterated their resolve to complete this task by 2012.

Setting up National Power Grid 
851. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government is going ahead with its reform 
strategy to set up a National Power Grid at a cost of Rs. 44,000 crore to 
50,000 crore; 
(b) whether the private sector will be investing in the development of 
this grid, however, control will continue to be with Government; and 
(c) if so, the details of this plan and the role of the private sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The Government is working 
on a plan to develop a National Power Grid connecting all the five regional 
grids with a strong transmission network. The various transmission 
components of the National Power Grid are targeted to be realized in a 
phased manner, by the end of 11th Plan period. The total investment required 
for the Central transmission system in the next 10 years is estimated to be of 
the order of Rs. 77,000 crore, of which about Rs. 47,000 crore would be 
required for the projects involving inter-regional transmission system and Rs. 
30,000 crore for regional transmission schemes for power evacuation and 
system strengthening. 
The Electricity Laws were amended in 1998 to enable implementation 
of transmission projects by Centra l/State PowerTransmission utilities and 
also by private transmission companie s either on joint venture basis in 
association with Central/State Transmission Utility or independently as 
Independent Power Transmission Companies (IPTC) by obtaining 
transmission license from Central/State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions (CERC/SERC) depending on whether the transmission line/ 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
associated sub stations are inter-State or intra State. Of the total investment of Rs. 
77,000 crore for development of National Power Grid, about Rs. 23,000 crore 
is proposed to be mobilized through private sector participation by formation 
of joint ventures (JVs) with private entities and also through Independent Power 
Transmission Companies (IPTCs) which are proposed to be selected through 
International Competitive Bidding. The amended laws provide that a 
transmission license granted by CE RC/ SERC may authorize the licensee to 
construct, maintain and operate any inter-State transmission system or intra-State 
transmission system under the direction, control and supervision of the Central or 
State Transmission Utility, respectively. At present, Power Grid Corporation 
of India Ltd. (PGCIL) has been notified by the Government of India as the 
Central Transmission Utility. The Central/State Transmission Utility shall 
exercise supervision and control over the inter-State and intra-State transmission 
systems, respectively.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject: Introduction of revised Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) 
The Government had announced a Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) 
vide OM No. 2(36)/86-BPE (WC) dated 5th October, 1988. Government have 
revised the scheme to make it more efficacious having regard to both, the 
interests of the employees and the need to enable public Sector Enterprises 
(PSEs) to rationlize their surplus manpower. 
2. Enterprises which are financially sound and can sustain a scheme of VRS 
on their own surplus resources may devise and implement variants of the existing 
VRS cited in para 1 above. However, in no cases shall the compensation exceed 
60 days salary for each completed year of service or the salary for the number 
of months service left, whichever is less. Salary for the purpose of VRS shall 
consist of basic pay and DA only and no other element. 
3. Enterprises that make marginal profits or loss-making enterprises may 
adopt the revised scheme of VRS which is modelled on the Scheme that exists in 
the State of Gujarat. The details of the scheme are set out hereunder: 
162 

[24 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) The compensation will consist of salary of 35 days for every 
completed year of service and 25 days for the balance of service 
left untill superannuation. The Compensation will be subject to a 
minimum of Rs. 25,000/- or 250 days salary whichever is higher. 
However, this compensation shall not exceed the sum of salary that 
the employee would draw at the prevailing level for the balance of 
the period left before superannuation. 
(ii) Salary for purpose of VRS will consist of basic pay and DA only. 
(iii) Arrears of wages due to revi sion etc. will not be included in 
computing the eligible amount. 
(iv) Payment of bonus should conform to the provisions in the Bonus 
Act; Casual Leave may be encashed in proportionate measure upto 
the date of VRS. 
4. A suitable variant of the arrangement in para 3 above may be 
developed by the Ministry of Textiles in respect of Textile units subject to the 
conditions attached thereto. 
5. For sick and unviable units, the VSS package of Department of Heavy 
Industry will be adopted. As a corollary, the VSS scheme may be modelled on 
Gujarat pattern and be made applicable as in para 3 above. However employee 
would have to opt for VSS within 3 months from the date of offer failing 
which they would be eligible only for retrenchment compensation. The details 
of VSS are as under:— 
(i) An employee would be entitled to ex-gratia payment equivalent to 45 
days emoluments (Pay+DA) for each completed year of service of 
the monthly emolument at the time of retirement multiplied by the 
balance months of service left before the normal date of 
retirement, whichever is less; 
(ii) All those who have completed not less than 30 years of service, will be 
eligible for maximum of 60.(sixty) months salary-wage as 
compensation. This will be subj ect to the amount not exceeding 
the salary/wage for the balance period of service left at the rate of 
monthly salary/wage at the time of voluntary retirement. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
6. The compensation under VRS/VSS will be in addition to terminal 
benefits. 
7. Employees of industrial cooperatives with Government equity 
participation and who are not member of the cooperative will also be covered 
under the VRS. 
8. Budgetary support will be provided to  the marginally profit or loss 
making enterprises and to the sick enterprises for implementing VRS only in case 
bank credit is not available. The funds would normally be made available at 
the beginning of the financial year. However before seeking budgetary support 
in cases of unviable/sick PSUs other sources of funding should be fully explored 
such as asset securitisation and bank loans against Government guarantee for 
funding VRS/VSS. 
9.VRS will be applicable to the permanent employees, badli workers, work 
charged established and temporary workers but not to the casual workers. 
There will be no recruitment against vacancies arising due to VRS. 
10. It will be the responsibility of the concerned administrative Ministry to 
assist those opting for VRS in getting loans from banks for pursuing gainful 
self employment. 
11. NRF in its present form will cease to  exist. The fund s required for 
retraining/rehabilitation of employees availing of VRS will be placed with the 
Department of Public Enterprises under arrangements to be evolved. 
12. In implementing the VRS scheme, managements shall ensure that it 
is extended primarily to such emoloyees whose services may be dispensed 
without detriment to the company. Care will be exercised to ensure that highly 
skilled and qualified workers and staff are not given the option. As there shall be 
no recruitment against vacancies arising due to VRS-it is important that 
organization is not denuded of talent. The managements of the PSUs shall 
introduce the VRS with the approval of their Boards and the administrative 
Ministries. 
13. The administrative Ministries/Departments are requested to bring the 
details of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme and the Voluntary Separation Scheme to 
the notice of the Public Enterprises under their administrative control and to 
ensure that PSEs implement the sche mes strictly in accordance with the 
provision set out herein.

Subject:   Further modification in the revised Voluntary Retirement Scheme. 
The Government have decided further to modify, with immediate effect, 
the Revised Voluntary Retirement Scheme for Central PSUs introduced vide this 
Department's O.M. of even number dated 5th May, 2000 as under:— 
(a) Ex-gratia payment in respect of employees on pay scajes at   . 1.1.87

extant scheme, shall be increased by 100% and 50% respectively.

employees of marginally profit/loss making, as well as sick and unviable units.

(c) Under the Gujarat pattern, the salary for VRS/VSS shall be 
calculated on the basis of 30 days in a month and not 26 days. Consequently, 
the method of calculation of ex-gratia for VRS and VSS shall be similar. 
 
(d) Once an employee avails himself of voluntary retirement from a 
PSU, he shall not be allowed to take up imployment in another PSU. If he 
desires to do so, he shall have to re turn the VRS compensation received by 
him to the PSU concerned. Where th e compensation was paid out of a 
Government grant, the PSU concerned shall remit the refunded amount to the 
Government. In case the PSU is already closed/ merged, the VRS 
compensation shall be returned directly to the Government. 
 
2. All other provisions of the DPE guideliness dated 5.5.2000 are to 
continue. 
3. The clarifications given in the DPEs O.M. of even number dated 8th 
December, 2000 stand modified in consequence of the foregoing. 
4. The employees, who have already been  released by the PSU's before 
the date of issue of this O.M. shall not be covered under the modified scheme. 
5. The administrative Ministries/Departments are required to bring the 
modified VRS/VSS to the notice of the public enterprises under their 
administrative control and ensure strict compliance with the provisions of the 
scheme.

Need to take necessary steps for permanent solution to power 
and water crisis 
PROF. M.M. AGARWAL (Uttar Pradesh): Hon. Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to draw your kind attent ion to the acute shortage of power and 
water being faced by the people in differe nt parts of the country, particularly in 
the metropolitan cities. In fact, the powe r situation in various parts of country 
is not going to improve despite priv atisation of the power sector. The 
Government had made tall claims of improving the situation, but all attempts 
in this regard have proved fruitless. Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, 
Orissa. the NCR States, have all had to face acute power shortage during the 
present Monsoon season. Many cities have gone without power continuously, 
for long hours. The people in the metropolitan cities have been facing water 
shortage. For the past one month, the water supply has not been normal. The 
supply of drinking water has considerably reduced. Muddy water is being 
supplied. The distribution of water is so  faulty that most of the families, 
residing in Government colonies, in the metropolitan cities, are not getting 
even their minimum requirement. Despite the installation of booster-pumping 
stations in various colonies, people are not getting adequate water supply. 
Power-cuts and low voltage have disrupt ed the functioning of vital water 
installations in these cities. This has seriously affected the water supply to 
various colonies in these cities. Most of the residents have had no water, 
because water treatment plants have no  power, or the voltage has been so 
low that they are not working. The St ate Governments/ Union Territories and 
the authorities have no effective scheme in this respect. Therefore, I would 
like to urge upon the Central Government to take effective measures, and 
necessary directions should be given to the concerned States and authorities 
to find out a permanent solution to the serious power and water crisis being 
faced by the country.

SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominat ed): Mr. Chairman, "Sir, since 
Yesterday, we have all been letting off much steam on this Short Duration 
Discussion, but article 355 has been overtaken by the events as Pranabda, 
very frankly, said whilst initiating the discussion yester. Even before this 
discussion started, the spotlight was on the Election Commission. It is still on 
the Election Commission, the exclusive constitutional functionary set up to 
conduct elections. Now, the Assembly has been dissolved by the Governor, 
and the stage is set for the operation of Section 15(2) of the Representation of 
People's Act. That section says: 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
"That the Governor shall, by one or more Notifications, published in 
the Gazette on such date or dates as may be recommended by the Election 
Commission, call upon all the constituencies in the State to elect members." 
What this House recommends, Sir, is neither here nor there, the date 
or dates for the elections are to be recommended by the Election 
Commissioner, and the State Governor's notification will have to say so. 
But, what if -- and that is a big 'if -- the Governor, which really means 
the State Government, issues the Notification despite the recommendations of 
the Election Commission to hold the elections at a date later than September 
or October. 
And, my respectful answer is, that a recommendation is never oral, it 
is in writing, and obviously the Election Commission will give reasons why it so 
recommends; and since nothing remains a secret in this country, -regrettably, 
not even Cabinet papers -- the country is bound to come to know ultimately 
what the Election Commission had recommended. 
Whatever it recommends, I would say to my hon. friends on my right 
that as you know and I know, elections are inevitable in Gujarat, whether in 
September or October or next February, and we cannot simply wish them 
away with speeches. If you do not win t he hearts of the people of Gujarat now, 
if you do not convince t hem that in Gandhiji's Gujarat Bapu was right in his 
concept of India and Godse was wrong, I am afraid, you will have lost the 
elections whether now or in next February. 
Sir, what article 174 of the Constitution says or does not say has, I 
believe become totally irrelevant, whatever lawyers may say. It will be for the 
court which will decide in God's good time, only after the elections, and not 
before. 
As for imposition of President's rule, under article 356, I believe, Sir, 
this is a wishful thinking. It has only once been imposed after an Assembly was 
dissolved in Kerala in 1970, and only when the care-taker Chief Minister, Shri 
Achutta Menon, actually resigned. If Sh ri Narendra Modi, the care-taker Chief 
Minister, is sporting and has the confidence in himself, he can do an Achutta 
Menon act, because after President's rule was imposed in Kerala and elections 
were held, Achutta Menon's party, the CPI, won and Achutta Menon became 
the Chief Minister again! 
Let us face the facts. Let us face reality. The Home Minister, now the  
Deputy  Prime  Minister,  has authoritatively  said  in the other House, 
178

yesterday, that elections are going to be held -- whether we wish it or do not 
wish it - and if you believe in democracy, as we must all, I would urge the hon. 
Members to realise that neither party can win elections in Gujarat. In this 
house, for this reason alone, the discussion has become sterile. 
But, having said this, I must also urge my friends on the Treasury 
Benches and those who support them that it is now time to lower the rhetoric. 
You may or you may not win elections in the short term by generating hate 
and causing anguish. But, believe me, you cannot and you will not, in the long 
run, win elections merely on policies of hate; you will win elections only on 
policies of performance. 
The hon. Member, the former Law Minister, Shri Arun Jaitley, said 
that they want to go back to the people. Well, the Governor has granted them 
this. But, remember, the triumph will not be if you win the elections. If you win 
the elections, you will have a BJP Government in Gujarat, but you already"

minority community voted for BJP. Then only, and then only, I believe, will the 
BJP become a mature political party in this country. 
I have many friends in the Government. I have great regard and 
respect for the hon. Deputy Prime Minister, whom I happen to know for more 
years than I can remember. Sir, we were opposing each other in the Supreme

carrying with us one hundred per cent of the population, whichever 
Government runs it. Let us not try to run it on the basis that there is a large 
segment of the population which is not with this country. I refuse, Sir, to accept 
this. Why not say frankly -- that is what I would have said -- "we have not yet 
restored the confidence amongst the minorities, but we are trying very hard." I 
was happy to see an interview by the new President of the BJP in this 
morning's Times of India. I hope he has been correctly reported. He said, and I 
quote: "We will make a special effort to get the minorities' support without 
compromising on our belief in justice for all and appeasement of none." I 
would say: 'Hear, hear; good.' Let us see more of this. Why not open a new 
chapter?    Make a special effort to win the support of the minorities,

I read yesterday that you are not letting Amnesty in. Why not?

word 'laundering' itself means 'clean ing'. And, the meaning of the money-

through any other activities like crimes, etc,  and if it is launder ed, i.e., if it is

the international level because, the money generated in one country goes to 
another country and then subsequently to the third country, fourth country, and 
it finally comes back to the original person who had generated that money.

economy, the normal activity of any industry because, when these money-
launderers or these black money owners br ing back that money, they use it in 
such a way that they can control the economy of a country, small or big.   So, 
this 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
is a very serious matter. Under no circumstances, one can say that the Bill to 
prevent money-laundering should not be accepted. It has to be accepted. I 
welcome the Bill. I support the Bill. But I would like to caution the Government. 
There is no question of opposing it. Nobody will say that money-laundering 
should be allowed. It goes without saying. Sir, you will be surprised to know 
that the scope of money-laundering in the world is two to five per cent of the 
total GDP, i.e., it is in billions and bill ions and billions of dollars. This is the 
volume of money-laundering all over t he world. In fact, the volume of the 
money laundered is much more than the volume of money in the real real 
economy. Therefore, you can understand the seriousness of the problem. Illicit 
trafficking in drugs and arms has taken a heavy toll of the economy of various 
countries. According to one estimate, the amount included in illegal trafficking 
in drugs is staggering --$5 billion per ye ar. The amount included in illicit trade 
in arms is again a staggering. It is $7 bi llion. This is the volume of the money 
laundered all over the world. 
Sir, we have the Golden Crescent comprising Afghanistan, Pakistan 
and Iran. Similarly, we have the Golden Triangle, comprising Myanmar, Laos 
and Thailand. As far as trafficking in dr ugs is concerned, India, unfortunately, 
has been a transit country. The Purulia case of illegal trade in arms is  very 
well known.   So, we in India, have to be very very careful. 
Now, how did this question of bringing in a Bill on money laundering 
come in? In 1998, there was a United Na tions Convention against Illicit Traffic 
in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances. The Vienna Convention of 
1988 provided a comprehensive legal definition of money laundering. This 
definition formed the basis of subseque nt legislations on money laundering 
laws in various countries. This Convention was held in 1988; but, in our 
country, somehow we started dealing with it in 1998 - ten years afterwards. 
Therefore, it is high time to have such a legislation. 
The Brussels Statement of Principles enunciated in 1999, outlined the 
basic policies and procedures that banks should follow in order to assist the 
law-enforcing agencies in tackling the problem of money laundering. After that, 
a Financial Action Task Force (FATF) on money laundering was established at 
the G-7 Summit held in Paris in 1999, to address the global problem of money 
laundering.  They made 40 recommendations. 
228 

[24 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The latest initiative taken by the United Nations was at its Special 
Session on countering together the drug problem. The Session, which 
concluded in June 1998, made a declaration to deal firmly with money 
laundering.   After that, nothing much has happened. 
Like the NPT, this is also an international problem. This problem 
cannot be solved unless it is tackled by  all the. countries of the world. If 
countries like Pakistan, Burma, or even smaller countries like Nepal, Bhutan, 
Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, do not tackle this pr oblem, it will become very difficult 
for India to handle this situation independently. 
We have now well understood the necessity for an Act dealing with 
this problem. But my point is, have we provided enough safety clauses? Mr. 
Finance Minister, why I am talking of sa fety precautions is because of our 
experience in the case of POTA. You passed the POTA at a Joint Session with 
a lot of fanfare. At that time, we caut ioned you to be careful. We asked you to 
have some safety provisions in the Bill. But you did not want to listen. You 
know what has happened. Your own colleague has now fallen a victim of this 
POTA legislation, and you can do nothing.  Therefore, my question is, whether 
we are taking enough precautions in th is Bill. Maybe, you have accepted all 
the recommendations of the Select Comm ittee. Despite this, I would like to 
point out a few more things which you may like to consider. Sir, we have plenty 
of laws to deal with different crimes in the country. For the last fifty years or 
even before that, a number of laws have been enacted to deal with different 
crimes. And this is a super law on money-laundering where you have covered 
the laws which are under the other Acts also. If your intention is to have it only 
for terrorism, if your intention is to ha ve it only for narcotics and drugs, then, 
confine it to that only. You know how our system functions, how the police 
officers, how the other intelligence agencies, function. You can go to the court 
later. But the first stage is the constable or, maybe, a director. He reads the 
law; he decides the law which is enact ed here and takes action. And, once he 
takes action, the ordinary citizen of the country may suffer immensely. How 
many people do we have in the jails like that because of the different laws? 
Thousands and thousands are languishing in the jails for years and years. 
Nobody is there to look after them. If a similar situation arises because of this 
law, what safety precautions do we have  to ensure that these officers are not 
going to misuse this particular law also? 
In addition to the traditional banking institutions, anti-money-
laundering measures should apply as far as it is practicable to non-banking 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
financial institutions and other professi ons or enterprises which may be used 
for money-laundering. I have no objection to this. I think this is one of the 
recommendations of the Select Committee also. Since you have said that you 
have accepted them, it is good. But, professional associations should be urged 
to exclude from their membership those who are involved in money-laundering. 
Even this is very important. You can make the law, but the implementation is 
not that easy. Unless every citizen is tu tored, is made familiar about these 
laws, it is difficult. These associations have to know all these things. They have 
to be told that they also have to he lp you. Then only this kind of a law will 
become a success. 
States should consider measures  which would make alternative 
remittance systems, where they are not prohibited (Hawala, etc.), subject to 
the same anti-money-laundering rules as other financial institutions, for the 
purpose of preventing their abuse by money-launderers. It is applicable not 
only in our country, but in the nearby countries also. If Hawala continues in any 
form, money-laundering will also continue in bigger amounts. That is why this 
kind of situations involving a volume of 700 billion dollars or 500 billion dollars 
arise. We have to stop Hawala transactions by any method. Then only this law 
will be meaningful. 
Government and international, organisations should take measures to 
sensitise the public, legislators, policy-makers and the media with regard to the 
dangers posed by money-laundering. 
Sir, I have already said, "Don't make it a police State". I am not 
repeating it. A number of Chambers have come to me also. A number of 
people have visited ordinary citizens and they say that a person can be picked 
up on suspicion of indulging in money-laundering and acquiring property with 
that money and the offence is non-bailabl e until the appellate authority decides 
the case. Besides, the onus of proving his innocence is on the suspect. This 
could well mean that people would remain behind bars till the appellate 
authority decides the case, as an appeal to the High Court was possible only 
after the appellate authority delivered its judgment. 
I would like to know one thing from the hon. Finance Minister. What 
precautions do we have against the fear of unwarranted arrest, which is a big 
issue in the minds of the ordinary  citizens? Sir, there are forty 
recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force. I am not going to 
mention all the recommendations. I would like to quote a few of them which are 
internationally required. I would quote the selected recommendations. 
230 

[24 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
"Firstly, each country should take immediate steps to ratify and to 
implement fully, the 1988 United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in 
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (the Vienna Convention)." 
The next recommendation is: "Wherever possible, corporations 
themselves-not only their employees-- should be subject to criminal liability. 
But, whatever has happened in the corporate world of America, the 
corporation itself is equally responsible." 
Now, according to me, the next recommendation is very important. It 
says: "Financial institutio ns should pay special attention to all complex, 
unusual large transactions, and all unusual patterns of transactions, which 
have ..no apparent economic or visible lawful purpose." I would like to 
underline the words--"unusual large transactions and all unusual patterns of 
transactions. " The background and purpose of such transactions should, as 
far as possible, be examined, the findi ngs established in writing, and be 
available to help supervisors, auditors and law enforcement agencies." 
The next recommendation says that "the financial institutions should 
develop programs against money laundering. These programs should include, 
as a minimum:- 
(i). the   development   of   inte rnal   policies,   procedures   and 
controls, including the designation of compliance officers at 
management level, and adequate screening procedures to 
ensure high standards when hiring employees. 
(ii) an on-going employee training programme; 
(iii) an audit function to the system." 
Obviously, we do not want to have audi tors like Anderson. We want auditors 
who are genuinely doing their job. We need to cope with the problem of 
countries with no or insufficient anti-money laundering measures. Sir, being an 
ex-Foreign Minister, I am sure you have a lot of influence around the 
countries, and with your efforts, a lot of improvement can be made. 
The next recommendation is that "t he financial institutions should 
ensure that the principles mentioned above are also applied to the branches 
and majority owned subsidiaries located abroad, especially, in countries which 
do not or insufficiently apply these re commendations, to the extent that local 
applicable laws and regulations permit. When the local applicable 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
laws and regulations prohibit this implementation, competent authorities in that 
country of the mother institution should be informed by the financial institutions 
that they cannot apply these recommendations." 
The last recommendation, out of the selected forty recommendations, 
is this: 
"Each country should make efforts to improve a spontaneous or 
"upon request" international information exchange relating to 
suspicious transactions, persons and corporations involved in those 
transactions between competent authorities. Strict safeguards should 
be established to ensure that this exchange of information is 
consistent with national and inter national provisions on privacy and 
data protection." 
Sir, when we talk about the report of the Select Committee, I am 
sure, we are talking about the recommendations of the second Select 
Committee. I do not know which Committee it is. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI): The hon. Minister 
has clarified the dates. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Probably, it is the Second Committee. 
On page 25, item No. 15, clause 2, a reference has been made to the offence 
specified under part (b) of the Schedule. It says:" If the total value involved in 
such offences is Rs. 30 lakhs or  more..." According to me, this 
recommendation of Rs. 30 lakhs is, probably, one or two years old. Today, the 
value of Rs.1 crore is less than even Rs.30 lakhs. The purchasing power of 
Rs.1 crore today is less than that of Rs .30 lakhs, that too, two years before. 
So, I request that this amount should be in creased to Rs.1 crore; otherwise, it 
will be impossible for all the financial instit utions to keep that kind of record. 
Industries are put up with an investment  of Rs. 10,000 crores. One industry 
invests Rs.1,000 crores; others are investing Rs.2,000 crores, Rs.3,000 
crores, etc. Therefore, this amount of  Rs.30 lakhs is meaningless.   Please 
increase it to, at least, Rs.1 crore. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI): You have spoken 
at great length.  There are other Members also.   Please wind up now. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Now, clause 12(1): 
232 

[24 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
"Provided that where the principal officer of a banking company or 
financial institutions or intermediary, as the case may be, has reason 
to believe that a single transaction or series of transactions integrally 
connected to each other have bee n valued below the prescribed 
value so as to defeat the provisions of this section, such officer shall 
furnish information in respect of such transactions to the Director 
within the prescribed time." 
I fully support this clause, because the value is only notional. It does 
not mean that somebody is making a mischief with lower value; the officer 
knows that, but he will keep quiet, under the clause. I don't think that that is 
the intention of the Act, 
Then, I refer to clause 16.1 - power of survey. I can't understand why 
the word "survey" has been used. I c an understand if the words "search and 
seizure" have been used. If you have information, you can search, you can 
seize. But why do you want to survey? What kind of things you are going to 
survey? 
"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this 
Act, where an authority, on the basis of material in his possession, 
has reason to believe (the reasons for such belief to be recorded in 
writing) ...... " 
This is a good provision, Sir.  Everything has to be recorded in writing. 
" ....... that an offence under section 3 has been committed, he may 
enter any place— 
(iv) within the limits of the area assigned to him." 
But where is the survey required?   It is a clear-cut case of search.   If you 
change the word there, the problem would be solved. 
Now, I refer to clause 19(1) - power to arrest. The power to arrest is 
with the Director, Deputy Director, Assist ant Director or any other officer. This 
is so broad. The power to arrest, I should say, should be only with the Director 
or with the Deputy Director, and not wi th any other officer authorised by the 
Central Government. I am saying this, because any officer can go and arrest 
the person, and, then, get the power, the  authority, from the Director, to 
maintain the sanctity of that arrest. The words "any other officer" should be 
omitted. But "the reason for such belief to be recorded in writng" is a very 
good provision. 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July, 2002] 
Chapter IV :  APPELLATE TRIBUNAL. 
"Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may, after giving an opportunity 
of being heard, entertain an appeal after the expiry of the said period 
of forty-five days if it is satisf ied that there was sufficient cause for 
not filing it within that period." 
Tnis is a clause which we have seen for the .first time, because the 
Government never gives this kind of powers. It is a good clause for ordinary 
citizens. 
I then come to clause 62 - punishment for vexatious search. 
"Any authority or officer exercising powers under this Act or any 
rules made thereunder, who, without reasons recorded in 
writing ............ “ 
I think, for -the word "reason", the words "without reasonable reasons" should 
be substituted. I mean, the reasons whic h appear to be reasonable, at least. 
This is again very bad. One can put any reasons and say, "I have given my 
reasons in writing". Simply giving the reasons in writing is not enough. Valid 
reasons should be given. Then only the question of searching and detaining 
person would arise. It should not be done simply on doubts, or, giving reasons 
which are not valid. If it is so, the punishment provided is acceptable to me. 
The last point which I want to make is this. As I have stated earlier, 
originally, this particular Bill was meant for dealing with smuggling of narcotics 
and waging or attempting to wage or abetting to waging a war against the 
Government of India. I have no objection, if you include conspiracy to commit 
an offence punishable under certain sections. I don't know the sections. But 
the point is this. Beyond that, inclusion of Part B is superfluous. All these 
things are already there in the laws. Why do you want this Part B also? Of 
course, you can include the Arms Act.  You can include even Part A. The 
inclusion of the other things in the overall parameters of this Bill does not 
seem, to me, to be logical. This Bill will be a draconian Bill, unless these 
safety measures are taken. I, therefore, request the hon. Minister to look into 
these points. 
In the Bill, which was circulated to us before, there is a provision, 
"Provided further that where such property is held jointly by more than one 
person, such notice shall be served to all persons holding such property". It is 
a very normal practice to hold a property   by 10 or 15 or 20 persons 
234 

[24 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
jointly. If a partner doesn't have any way to find out what the other 19 people 
are doing, how can you hold him responsible? How can you hold the other 19 
people responsible for the acts of one person? So, this point has to be taken 
into consideration. We don't have any machinery to find out this. Is there any 
guarantee that if I give notice to the Government, they will give me the 
credentials of the other partners, before I enter into a partnership of this kind? 
If it is not there, how do I take the responsibility for the acts of somebody else? 
I don't think in today's world even the parents can't take the responsibility for 
the acts of their children. I know one case. I don't want to name him. Way 
back in 1980, the son of a big leader sm uggled something into the airport. He 
was the Chief Minister of some State at  that time. He disowned his son. He 
said, "He is not my son". How can you hold a person responsible for the acts 
of his son? This point also has to be taken into consideration. 
Similarly, the definition of "intermediary" includes a stock-broker, sub-
broker, share transfer agent, banker to an issue, trustee to a trust  deed, etc. I 
think we are trying to cover the entire thing. This particular Bill is specifically 
for the purpose of dealing with smuggling of narcotics. You can include things 
like waging a war against the Government or something very serious. The 
impact of these provisions will come down , if you make it so broad and bring 
any act that one does anywhere in the co untry under this Bill. Please don't do 
that. Please try to be more specific. For example, a Hindu undivided family 
includes wife, brother, son, etc. How  can you hold the wife responsible for the 
acts of the husband? They are differ ent individuals. How can you hold the 
husband responsible for the acts of the wife? In  Chapter II, Offence of Money-
Laundering, it is stated, "knowingly enters into any transaction which is related 
to proceeds of crime either directly or  indirectly". Again, you are covering the 
entire thing. What do you mean by 'indi rectly'? You would not be able to 
implement this kind of a law. If you im plement it, it would become vague. All 
the bureaucrats would take advantage of this law. 
I have already talked about the scheduled offences. I will take two 
minutes more. 
I come to clause 19(1). I will read only the operational part of clause 
19(1). It says, "...He may arrest such person and shall, as  soon as may be, 
inform him of the grounds for such arre st". Why should it be 'as soon as may 
be'? Why should you not give the grounds of  arrest at the time of arrest?    
You are going to arrest him on some grounds, not on 
235 

RAJYA SABHA [24 July. 2002] 
suspicion. Why should there be these words 'as soon as may be'? You are not 
saying, "In one day or two days or th ree days or one month or two months" 
You are simply saying. "As soon as may be". I would request you to consider 
it. The grounds of arrest should, in any case, be given at the time of arrest 
because every offence punishable under this Act shall be cognizable. The 
moment you decide that this is an o ffence under this Act, the first thing 
anybody will do in this country would be, he would arrest him without 
assigning any reason. Later on, he might say, "We did not have enough 
reasons. We are sorry. You can go ba ck". Even that can happen. Sir, you are 
looking at me with angry eyes.
